description: Our place in a barred spiral galaxy, the Local Group, Hubble's tuning-fork classification, and active galactic nuclei.
content_html:
Seeing the Milky Way

On a clear night away from light pollution, the Milky Way is visible as a faint, irregular band of light arching across the sky. This is not a separate object in space: it is our own galaxy, the Milky Way Galaxy, seen edge-on from our position within it. The band is broader and brighter towards the constellation Sagittarius, which lies in the direction of the galactic centre. Even with binoculars, the band resolves into countless individual stars and dark rifts of dust.

Structure of the Milky Way

The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy with several distinct components:

  • The disc — a flattened region containing most of the galaxy’s stars, gas, and dust, including the spiral arms. New star formation is concentrated in the disc. The disc is about 100,000 light-years across but only ~1,000 light-years thick.
  • The central bulge — a roughly spherical concentration of older stars at the galactic centre. At the very centre lies a supermassive black hole known as Sagittarius A*, with a mass of approximately 4 million solar masses.
  • The central bar — a bar-shaped concentration of stars passing through the galactic centre, from which the spiral arms emerge. This feature gives the Milky Way its classification as a barred spiral.
  • The halo — a roughly spherical volume surrounding the disc, populated by old stars and globular clusters (over 150 are known around the Milky Way). The halo also contains the majority of the galaxy’s dark matter.

The Sun is located about 26,000 light-years from the galactic centre, in the Orion Spur — a minor arm between two major spiral arms. The Sun takes about 225-250 million years to complete one orbit of the galactic centre (the galactic year).

Key Fact

The Milky Way’s four main structural components: disc (stars, gas, dust, spiral arms, ongoing star formation); bulge (old stars, supermassive black hole at centre); bar (stars extending from centre, anchoring spiral arms); halo (globular clusters, old stars, dark matter).

Mapping the Milky Way with the 21 cm Line

Visible light cannot penetrate the dense dust of the galactic disc, so optical telescopes cannot map the full structure of our galaxy. Radio waves, however, travel through dust unimpeded. Neutral hydrogen in the interstellar medium emits a characteristic radio wave at a wavelength of 21 cm. By measuring the Doppler shift of this emission in different directions, astronomers can map the distribution and velocity of hydrogen gas throughout the disc, revealing the galaxy’s spiral arm structure that would otherwise be hidden.

The Local Group

The Milky Way is not alone. It belongs to a gravitationally bound collection of galaxies called the Local Group, which contains roughly 80 galaxies spread across about 10 million light-years. The dominant members are:

  • Andromeda Galaxy (M31) — the largest galaxy in the Local Group, about 2.5 million light-years from Earth. It is a spiral galaxy slightly larger than the Milky Way and is approaching us at roughly 110 km/s. In about 4 billion years it will merge with the Milky Way.
  • Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) and Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) — irregular dwarf galaxies orbiting the Milky Way, visible in the Southern Hemisphere sky as separate misty patches. The LMC is about 160,000 light-years away.
  • Triangulum Galaxy (M33) — a smaller spiral galaxy about 2.7 million light-years away, the third-largest in the Local Group.

Hubble’s Galaxy Classification — the Tuning Fork

Edwin Hubble devised a classification system for galaxies, often illustrated as a Hubble tuning fork diagram. Galaxies are grouped by shape:

  • Elliptical galaxies (E0-E7) — smooth, featureless ellipses ranging from nearly circular (E0) to strongly flattened (E7). They contain mostly old red stars and little gas or dust, so star formation has effectively ceased.
  • Spiral galaxies (Sa-Sc) — disc galaxies with a central bulge and spiral arms containing young blue stars and active star formation. Sa spirals have tightly wound arms and a large bulge; Sc spirals have loosely wound arms and a smaller bulge.
  • Barred spiral galaxies (SBa-SBc) — like spirals but with a bar of stars through the centre from which the arms emerge. The Milky Way is classified as SBb.
  • Irregular galaxies — no regular shape; often the result of galactic collisions or gravitational disturbances. The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are examples.

Some galaxies have an exceptionally luminous nucleus powered by a active galactic nucleus (AGN). The energy comes from matter falling into the supermassive black hole, forming a hot accretion disc that can outshine the rest of the galaxy:

  • Seyfert galaxies: spiral galaxies with a bright, variable nucleus; the AGN is only a few times more luminous than the host galaxy. Their nuclei emit strongly in X-ray, UV and optical wavelengths.
  • Quasars (quasi-stellar objects): the most luminous AGN in the universe. They appear star-like in optical images but have enormous redshifts indicating they are billions of light-years away — meaning their luminosity must be extraordinary. Most quasars are seen at high redshift (ancient universe), consistent with the Big Bang model that the early universe was more active.
  • Blazars: AGN whose relativistic jet of particles happens to point almost directly at Earth. The jet’s emission is Doppler-boosted, making blazars appear extremely bright and highly variable across all wavelengths.

Galaxy groups and clusters are bound by gravity into larger structures. The Local Group is one of many groups within the Virgo Supercluster, which is itself part of the Laniakea Supercluster containing over 100,000 galaxies. On the largest scales, galaxies are distributed in a “cosmic web” of filaments, sheets and voids. Galaxy mergers — like the future Milky Way-Andromeda collision — are a key mechanism in galaxy evolution. When two spiral galaxies merge, the result is often a large elliptical galaxy in which star formation is disrupted and then quenched.

Key Fact

The Hubble tuning-fork classifies galaxies by visible shape: E0–E7 (ellipticals, round to elongated), Sa/Sb/Sc (spirals, tight to loose arms), SBa/SBb/SBc (barred spirals), and Irr (irregulars). The Milky Way is an SBc — a loose-armed barred spiral.
exam_tip_html: Questions on the Local Group most often ask you to name the three main galaxies and their types: Milky Way (barred spiral), Andromeda/M31 (spiral), and Triangulum/M33 (spiral); the Magellanic Clouds are irregular dwarfs. For questions on active galaxies, link the power source to the supermassive black hole’s accretion disc — do not just state “the black hole emits light” (black holes don’t; the accretion disc does). Quasars at high redshift are specific evidence for the Big Bang model that the early universe was different from today — this links to Lesson 14’s cosmology content.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy with four components: disc (stars, gas, dust, spiral arms); bulge (old stars, supermassive black hole); bar; halo (globular clusters, dark matter). The Sun is ~26,000 light-years from the centre.
  • Hubble classified galaxies as ellipticals (E0-E7), spirals (Sa-Sc), barred spirals (SBa-SBc) and irregulars. The Local Group contains the Milky Way, Andromeda (M31), Triangulum (M33) and the Magellanic Clouds.
  • Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are powered by supermassive black hole accretion. Types include Seyfert galaxies, quasars (the most luminous, seen at high redshift) and blazars (jets pointed at Earth). Neutral hydrogen’s 21 cm line maps galactic structure through dust.

practice_questions.text:
The Milky Way is classified as which type of galaxy?
A) Elliptical
B) Irregular
C) Barred spiral
D) Lenticular
State two members of the Local Group of galaxies other than the Milky Way, and give the galaxy type of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two of (one mark each for correct name + type pair):
• Andromeda Galaxy (M31) — spiral galaxy [1]
• Triangulum Galaxy (M33) — spiral galaxy [1]
• Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) — irregular galaxy [1]
• Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) — irregular galaxy [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain why radio astronomers use the 21 cm hydrogen line to map the structure of the Milky Way rather than using an optical telescope.
practice_questions.marks: Optical light is absorbed by dust clouds in the galactic disc, so optical telescopes cannot see through to the far side of the galaxy [1]. Radio waves at 21 cm pass through dust unimpeded [1]. Neutral hydrogen throughout the disc emits at 21 cm, and Doppler shifts in this emission reveal the hydrogen’s velocity, allowing mapping of the spiral arm structure [1].

practice_questions.text: Compare elliptical and spiral galaxies in terms of their star populations, ongoing star formation, and appearance through a telescope.
practice_questions.marks:
Elliptical galaxies:
• Contain mostly old, red stars with little gas or dust [1]
• Little or no ongoing star formation [1]
• Appear as smooth, featureless ellipses; no spiral arms or dust lanes visible [1]

Spiral galaxies:
• Contain both old stars in the bulge and young blue stars in the spiral arms [1]
• Active star formation in the spiral arms where gas and dust are plentiful [1]
• Show spiral arm structure and dust lanes through a telescope; nucleus is a bright point [1]

Mark up to 4: 1 per correct comparison point (max 2 per type).

practice_questions.text: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) has an apparent magnitude of +3.44 and an absolute magnitude of -21.5. Calculate its distance in parsecs using the distance modulus formula. Show all working.
practice_questions.marks:
Formula: m - M = 5 log10(d) - 5 [1]
Substitution: 3.44 - (-21.5) = 5 log10(d) - 5 → 24.94 = 5 log10(d) - 5 [1]
Rearrangement: log10(d) = (24.94 + 5) / 5 = 29.94 / 5 = 5.988 [1]
Answer: d = 10^5.988 ≈ 970,000 parsecs (accept 10^6 = 1,000,000 pc for M = -21.5 rounded) [1]
(Note: actual distance to M31 is ~770 kpc; accept any answer consistent with correct working from the given magnitudes.)

practice_questions.text:
Niamh O'Sullivan, an astronomer at a university in Dublin, is presenting to the Caerwyn Observatory astronomy club in Wales on the topic of quasars and what they tell us about the history of the universe.

Evaluate the evidence from quasars that supports the Big Bang model of the universe, including: what quasars are and how they produce their luminosity, why their high redshifts are significant, and what the distribution of quasars across cosmic time implies about the early universe.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Quasars are the most luminous AGN, powered by supermassive black hole accretion discs; explains why the accretion disc (not the black hole itself) is the source; most quasars have very high redshifts placing them at enormous distances and therefore very early in cosmic history (looking back in time); the high number density of quasars at high redshift shows the early universe had more active galactic nuclei, implying the universe has changed over time; this directly contradicts the Steady State model (which predicts the universe looks the same at all epochs) and supports the Big Bang; fewer quasars in the nearby (recent) universe means they faded as black holes ran out of fuel and the universe aged.

Secure (3-4): Correctly describes quasars as luminous AGN; explains high redshift = great distance = early universe; states quasar distribution supports Big Bang over Steady State but may not explain the mechanism fully.

Developing (1-2): Some correct identification of quasars; limited link to Big Bang evidence.

Emerging (0): Irrelevant or no response.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the name of the supermassive black hole at the centre of the Milky Way?
In the Hubble galaxy classification scheme, an elliptical galaxy that is almost perfectly circular would be labelled:
The Milky Way is mapped in radio wavelengths using the 21 cm emission of neutral _____ gas.
The Milky Way is classified as a barred spiral, code _____b, meaning it has moderately wound arms.
Match each galaxy or galaxy group to its correct description.
right: Largest galaxy in the Local Group; spiral; ~2.5 million ly away
Irregular dwarf galaxy orbiting the Milky Way; ~160,000 ly away
Third-largest galaxy in the Local Group; spiral; ~2.7 million ly away

flashcard_questions.q: What are the four main structural components of the Milky Way?
flashcard_questions.a: Disc, central bulge, central bar, and halo.

flashcard_questions.q: How far is the Sun from the galactic centre?
Why is the 21 cm hydrogen line used to map the Milky Way rather than visible light?
flashcard_questions.a: Radio waves at 21 cm pass through dust unimpeded, whereas visible light is absorbed by galactic dust clouds.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the two largest members of the Local Group.
flashcard_questions.a: The Milky Way and the Andromeda Galaxy (M31).

flashcard_questions.q: What type of galaxies are the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds?
flashcard_questions.a: Irregular dwarf galaxies orbiting the Milky Way.

flashcard_questions.q: What does an E7 elliptical galaxy look like compared to an E0?
flashcard_questions.a: E7 is strongly flattened; E0 is nearly circular in appearance.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an active galactic nucleus (AGN)?
flashcard_questions.a: An extremely luminous compact region at a galaxy's centre, powered by matter accreting onto a supermassive black hole.

flashcard_questions.q: What makes quasars significant as evidence for the Big Bang?
flashcard_questions.a: Their high redshifts show they existed mainly in the early universe, proving the universe has changed over time, contradicting the Steady State model.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Hubble tuning fork diagram?
flashcard_questions.a: Hubble's classification of galaxies by shape: ellipticals (handle), spirals and barred spirals (two prongs), irregulars excluded.

flashcard_questions.q: What component of the Milky Way contains most of its dark matter?
What will happen when the Milky Way and Andromeda Galaxy eventually merge?
flashcard_questions.a: A large elliptical galaxy will likely form, with star formation disrupted by the collision.

glossary_terms.definition: The barred spiral galaxy containing our Solar System, approximately 100,000 light-years across, with the Sun located about 26,000 light-years from the galactic centre.
An extremely massive black hole (millions to billions of solar masses) found at the centre of most large galaxies, including Sagittarius A* at the Milky Way's centre.
A densely packed, spherical collection of hundreds of thousands of old stars orbiting the galactic centre in the galaxy's halo.
The gravitationally bound group of about 80 galaxies containing the Milky Way, dominated by the Milky Way and Andromeda.
Hubble's morphological classification of galaxies into ellipticals (E0-E7), spirals (Sa-Sc) and barred spirals (SBa-SBc), illustrated as a fork shape.
An extremely luminous compact region at a galaxy's centre powered by matter accreting onto a supermassive black hole.
Hydrogen gas in its ground state emitting radio waves at a wavelength of 21 cm, used to map the distribution of gas and spiral arms in the Milky Way.
A quasi-stellar object; the most luminous type of active galactic nucleus, observed predominantly at high redshift (early universe).
